articles.title: What to do when your foot is overheating
articles.dek: A warm foot is usually your body shedding heat. A foot that keeps climbing is a reason to act. Here's what to do in the next five minutes.

image.alt: A Georgia National Guard soldier soaked with water during annual training in record heat.
image.caption: On their first day at Fort Stewart, in 107° heat, Georgia Guard soldiers worked in the shade and doused themselves with water.

blocks.text: Your feet are built to dump heat. When you get hot, your body opens the blood vessels in the skin of your hands and feet and sends warm blood there to cool it. During heat stress, blood flow to the skin can reach six to eight litres a minute (Charkoudian, 2003). So a warm foot, on its own, is your body doing its job.

What matters is the pattern. A foot that keeps climbing while you work, or stays hot after you stop, can mean you're gaining heat faster than you can lose it. Hot ground, heavy boots and thick socks make that worse, because they trap the heat your feet are trying to shed.
What Thermyx is watching

Your insole measures the temperature where your foot touches it, not your core temperature. Thermyx raises its level to Caution when that reading reaches 38 °C (100.4 °F), when it rises fast, or when it runs well above what's usual for you. At 40 °C (104 °F) the insole stops heating on its own, whatever the app asks, to protect your skin.

blocks.title: In the next five minutes
items: Slow down or stop. Moving makes heat; resting stops adding to it.
Get into shade or air conditioning.
Switch the insoles to Cool, or leave them on Auto.
Loosen your boots, or take them off for a few minutes if it's safe to.
Drink water. About a cup every 15 to 20 minutes is the usual guidance when working in heat (Jacklitsch et al., 2016).

blocks.text: When it's more than a hot foot

Watch the whole person, not just the foot. Heavy sweating, dizziness, headache, nausea, cramps, weakness or fainting are signs of heat illness. Confusion, slurred speech, a seizure or collapse can mean heat stroke, which is an emergency.
When in doubt, cool the worker and call 911.

OSHA's first-aid guidance is to cool someone quickly, ideally by putting them in cold water or an ice bath, and to call for help (Occupational Safety and Health Administration, n.d.). Sports medicine guidance puts it as cool first, transport second, because the time spent hot is what does the damage (Casa et al., 2015).

blocks.title: What Thermyx can't do
blocks.text: Thermyx can't tell you whether you have heat illness. It shows how your feet are trending so you can act sooner. If someone is confused or collapses, call 911.

articles.title: How footwear fit can change pressure patterns
articles.dek: Most people's shoes don't fit their feet. Where your weight lands depends on it, and so do blisters, calluses and sore arches.

image.alt: The worn soles of three hiking shoes, side by side.
image.caption: Hiking shoes retired after 3,300 kilometres. Wear on a sole shows where your weight lands.

blocks.text: Stand barefoot and your heels take most of your weight. In a classic study of 107 symptom-free feet, the heel carried about 60 percent of the load, the forefoot about 28 percent and the midfoot about 8 percent, and peak pressure under the heel was about two and a half times that under the forefoot (Cavanagh et al., 1987).

Shoes change that picture. A shoe that's too short or too narrow concentrates pressure on the toes and the sides of the foot. One that's too loose lets the foot slide, which adds friction. And most of us are in the wrong size: across the studies in one review, 63 to 72 percent of people wore shoes that didn't match the width or length of their feet, and poor fit went with foot pain, corns, calluses and toe deformities (Buldt & Menz, 2018).
of your standing weight lands on your heels.
Friction, moisture and blisters

Blisters form when skin is rubbed back and forth under load, and moist skin makes the friction worse (Knapik et al., 1995). That's why hot, sweaty feet in loose boots blister so easily. Weight adds to it: carrying a pack raises the forces your feet take with every step and is linked with blisters and other foot problems (Knapik et al., 2004).
What your insole can tell you

Each Thermyx insole has one pressure sensor, under the arch. It can't map your whole sole, but it can show change: an arch loading more than usual, or one foot carrying clearly more than the other for minutes at a time. Thermyx flags a sustained left–right difference, because favouring one foot often goes with a fit problem, a sore spot or tiredness.

Sensors like this one drift under a steady load and read differently while loading and unloading (Abdul Razak et al., 2012). That's why Thermyx shows arch load as a level, not as a weight in kilograms.

blocks.title: Check your fit
items: Try shoes on at the end of the day, when your feet are largest.
Leave about a thumb's width between your longest toe and the end of the shoe.
The widest part of your foot should sit at the widest part of the shoe, without bulging over the sole.
Wear the socks you'll work in, and choose ones that wick moisture.
Lace so the heel stays put without squeezing the top of your foot.

blocks.title: If you have diabetes
blocks.text: Pressure matters more when feet have less feeling. High pressure under a numb foot can lead to ulcers, and relieving it is a core part of treatment (Bus et al., 2020). See a clinician about your footwear; don't rely on an app.

articles.title: Why recovery matters after heat exposure
articles.dek: The shift ends; the strain doesn't, at least not right away. What to do in the hours after a hot day so tomorrow starts even.

image.alt: Marines sit together on desert ground after a day of training.
image.caption: Marines talk through the day's training at Twentynine Palms, California, during Exercise Desert Scimitar 2015.

blocks.text: Working hard in the heat costs more than sweat. Active people can lose 4 to 10 litres of water and 3,500 to 7,000 milligrams of sodium a day in hot weather, and both have to be put back before the body is fully hydrated again (Shirreffs & Sawka, 2011).

If you have a day off, ordinary meals and drinks usually take care of it. If you're back at work within 24 hours, or you lost a lot of fluid, the same review recommends drinking deliberately and taking in electrolytes rather than waiting for thirst (Shirreffs & Sawka, 2011).
Why it matters for tomorrow

Starting a shift short on water puts more strain on your heart and raises your body temperature for the same work, and it makes hard work harder (Shirreffs & Sawka, 2011). The deficit you go to bed with is the one you wake up with.

blocks.title: After a hot shift
items: Drink with your next meals, and keep drinking through the evening.
Eat salty food or use an electrolyte drink if you sweated heavily.
Cool down: shade, a cool shower, or cool water on your skin.
Weigh yourself before and after work. The difference is mostly fluid, and it tells you how much to put back (American College of Sports Medicine et al., 2007).
Get your feet out of your boots, and let socks and liners dry.

blocks.text: What Thermyx shows
After an elevated reading, Home shows your foot-temperature trend. A foot cooling back toward your usual is a good sign. But it's only your feet: it can't show whether you've replaced what you lost.

blocks.title: When to get help
blocks.text: If you still feel unwell after rest and fluids, or your urine is dark like tea or cola, get medical help. Dark urine after hard work in heat can be a sign of muscle breakdown (Occupational Safety and Health Administration, n.d.).

references: American College of Sports Medicine, Sawka, M. N., Burke, L. M., Eichner, E. R., Maughan, R. J., Montain, S. J., & Stachenfeld, N. S. (2007). articles.title: How to recognize when sensor data may be unreliable
articles.dek: A reading is only as good as its contact, its battery and its connection. How to spot a bad one, and what Thermyx does about it.

image.alt: A researcher holds a thermistor probe against the tire of a car.
image.caption: A thermistor, the same kind of sensor that's in your insole, measures a running tire. National Institute of Standards and Technology.

blocks.text: Every temperature Thermyx shows comes from a small thermistor inside the insole, and every load from a force sensor. Small skin-temperature sensors like these can be accurate enough for research (Smith et al., 2010). But a reading is only as good as the sensor's contact with your foot, and a shift is messier than a lab.
Five signs a reading may be off

items: A flat line. Feet warm and cool as you move. A temperature that hasn't changed by a tenth of a degree for many minutes while you're active suggests a stuck sensor or a lost connection.
A jump your body couldn't make. A foot can't go from 30 to 38 °C in a few seconds. A sudden step usually means the insole shifted, or the sensor lost and regained contact.
Readings when you're not wearing it. An insole in your hand, on a car seat or by a heater reports that, not your foot.
A low battery or weak signal. Each insole's battery and connection strength are under Safety, then Device.
Only one foot. With one insole, Thermyx loses the left–right comparison, so a one-sided problem can go unseen.

blocks.text: Temperature isn't one number

Skin temperature differs from place to place and moves with the air around you, and none of it is the same as your core temperature (Taylor et al., 2014). Thermyx reports the temperature where your foot meets the insole. That's useful for spotting change and for comparing your feet, but it isn't your body temperature.

Pressure sensors have quirks too. Force-sensitive resistors drift under a steady load and read differently while loading and unloading (Abdul Razak et al., 2012), which is why arch load is shown as a level rather than a weight.
What Thermyx does

When a value is missing, Thermyx shows a dash, never an estimate. An insole that stops reporting drops off the screen instead of lingering as if it were live, and the widgets say when they last heard from your insoles. If something looks wrong, reseat the insole flat in your shoe, check the battery, and re-pair it from Safety, then Device.

blocks.title: Trust how you feel
blocks.text: If your readings look wrong and you feel unwell, believe your body over the app. Stop, cool down and get help.

articles.title: Heat illness: the signs, from cramps to heat stroke
articles.dek: Heat illness is a spectrum, and the dangerous end can arrive fast. Learn the signs, and the one response that matters most.

image.alt: Two emergency medical technicians drink water and wipe away sweat in the heat.
image.caption: Emergency medical technicians take water in the New Orleans heat, August 31, 2005.

blocks.text: Heat illness runs from a rash and muscle cramps to fainting, heat exhaustion and heat stroke. OSHA lists them together for a reason: their symptoms overlap and can appear at the same time. Its guidance is to give first aid as soon as any of them appear, rather than trying to work out which one it is (Occupational Safety and Health Administration, n.d.).
Know the signs

items: Heat cramps: muscle pain or spasms, usually in the legs, arms or trunk.
Heat syncope: fainting or dizziness.
Heat exhaustion: heavy sweating, tiredness, thirst, irritability, nausea or vomiting, dizziness, a fast heart rate.
Heat stroke: confusion, slurred speech, seizures or unconsciousness. The skin may be hot and dry, or still sweating heavily.

blocks.text: Heat stroke is an emergency

In heat stroke the body's temperature climbs above about 40 °C (104 °F) and the brain starts to fail. It can damage organs and kill (Epstein & Yanovich, 2019). The treatment is to cool the person as fast as possible. Cold-water immersion cools faster than other field methods (McDermott et al., 2009), and where people are cooled in cold water straight away, nearly all of them survive (Casa et al., 2007).
Cool first, transport second.

Sports medicine guidance is to cool someone with suspected exertional heat stroke on the spot, aiming to bring their temperature below about 39 °C (102.5 °F) within 30 minutes of collapse, before moving them (Casa et al., 2015). Call 911 straight away and keep cooling while you wait.
Where Thermyx fits

Thermyx watches how your feet trend and how steadily you walk. At High risk it tells your trusted circle and locks out heating. At Critical it opens a full-screen alert with an SOS button. It can't measure your core temperature, and it can't tell heat exhaustion from heat stroke. If you see the signs above, act on them, whatever the app says.

articles.title: Cold feet, frostbite and how to warm up safely
articles.dek: In the cold your body protects your core by giving up your toes. How to keep feet warm, and what to do if they freeze.

image.alt: A pair of hiking boots on snowy ground.
image.caption: Hiking boots at Revelstoke Mountain Resort, British Columbia.

blocks.text: When you get cold, your body narrows the blood vessels in your skin, especially in your hands and feet, to keep heat in your core (Castellani & Young, 2016). It's a good trade for your organs and a bad one for your toes: with less warm blood reaching them, they cool toward the temperature of your boots.
Wet makes it worse. Sweat or snow in a boot soaks the insulation and draws heat out of the foot. So does standing still: walking warms your feet, and standing watch in the snow doesn't.
Frostbite

Frostbite is tissue freezing. Early on, skin goes numb and pale; deeper injury leaves it hard and waxy. The Wilderness Medical Society's guidance for rewarming frostbite is a warm, not hot, water bath at 37 to 39 °C (98.6 to 102.2 °F) until the skin is soft and pliable, then letting it air-dry (McIntosh et al., 2019).

blocks.title: If your feet may be frostbitten
items: Get to shelter, and get medical help.
Don't rub the skin, and don't warm it at a fire or heater: numb skin burns easily.
Don't thaw a foot that might freeze again before you reach care. Refreezing does more harm than staying frozen (McIntosh et al., 2019).
If help is far away and the foot won't refreeze, rewarm it in warm water as above.

blocks.text: How Thermyx helps

Thermyx raises its level to Caution when your foot reads 25 °C (77 °F) or lower, and Auto or Heat warms it gradually toward your target. Cold never locks out heating the way heat does, because warming is what a cold foot needs. The insole won't heat above 40 °C (104 °F), but warmth on numb skin can still burn, so if you've lost feeling in your feet, warm them slowly and check your skin.

blocks.title: Frostbite needs care
blocks.text: Thermyx can show a cold foot. It can't tell you whether tissue is freezing. Numb, white or hard skin needs medical attention.

articles.title: Water, rest, shade: hydration on the job
articles.dek: Thirst comes late. A simple schedule keeps you ahead of it, and a bathroom scale can tell you whether it's working.

image.alt: A volunteer holds out cups of water to passing runners.
image.caption: A volunteer hands water to runners during an Air Force half-marathon.

blocks.text: Sweat is how you cool. When people do physical work, sweat output often runs ahead of what they drink, and the deficit can hurt productivity and safety on the job (Kenefick & Sawka, 2007).
NIOSH recommends that workers in the heat drink about a cup (8 ounces) of water every 15 to 20 minutes, rather than waiting until they're thirsty (Jacklitsch et al., 2016).

blocks.title: A schedule that works
items: Start hydrated: drink with breakfast.
About a cup every 15 to 20 minutes while you work in the heat.
Take breaks in the shade, and drink during them.
On long, sweaty shifts, add an electrolyte drink or salty snacks.
Don't overdo it. Drinking far more than you sweat can dilute the sodium in your blood, which is dangerous too (American College of Sports Medicine et al., 2007).

blocks.text: Know your own sweat

Sweat rates vary a lot from person to person. The American College of Sports Medicine suggests weighing yourself before and after activity: each kilogram you lose is about a litre of fluid you didn't replace (American College of Sports Medicine et al., 2007).
Where Thermyx fits

Thermyx can't measure hydration. It can show your feet warming faster than usual and your steps getting less steady, both of which can come with heat strain. Treat a rising level as a prompt to drink and rest, not as a reading of how much water you need.

articles.title: Your first days in the heat are the riskiest
articles.dek: Bodies adapt to heat, but not overnight. Why new workers are most at risk, and how to build up safely.

image.alt: A soldier with a heavy pack walks alone down a road on a ruck march.
image.caption: A soldier on a ruck march in Vilseck, Germany, June 2020.

blocks.text: When federal investigators reviewed heat-related enforcement cases from 2012 and 2013, 13 involved a worker's death. Nine of those deaths happened in the worker's first three days on the job, and the employers' heat plans made no provision for helping new workers adjust (Arbury et al., 2014).
worker heat deaths in one federal review came in the first three days on the job.

That adjustment is called acclimatization. Over repeated days of work in the heat, you start sweating sooner and more, your heart rate and body temperature run lower for the same effort, and you hold on to more salt. Most of the change comes in the first week, and it's largely complete in about two (Périard et al., 2015; Racinais et al., 2015).
Build up gradually

NIOSH recommends that a new worker spend no more than 20 percent of the usual time in the heat on the first day, adding no more than 20 percent a day after that. Workers with recent experience can start at 50 percent, then 60, 80 and 100 percent over four days (Jacklitsch et al., 2016).
The benefit fades with time away from the heat, so ease back in after a break, an illness or a stretch of cool weather.
Where Thermyx fits

Thermyx learns your usual foot temperature during calibration and raises Caution when you run well above it. In your first days, take that seriously: you have less margin now than you will in two weeks.
